person/matthias-corvinus.observer: The Observer notes that Matthias's centralizing reforms rested heavily on his own standing army and personal authority rather than on durable institutions, so that much of his state-building unraveled within a generation of his death — a pattern common among strong rulers who do not also build the architecture that outlasts them.
questions: How much of the Bibliotheca Corviniana reflected Matthias's own intellectual interests, and how much reflected the prestige-collecting expected of any Renaissance monarch?

person/menelik-ii.summary: Menelik II (1844 to 1913) reigned as emperor of Ethiopia from 1889, and led the forces that defeated Italy at Adwa in 1896.
facts: He expanded the empire southward and founded Addis Ababa as its capital.
He imported modern arms and pursued the technological modernization of his state.
On 1 March 1896 he won the Battle of Adwa.
His empire's expansion came through the conquest of neighboring peoples, and how to judge that expansion is debated.
person/menelik-ii.context: Menelik led Ethiopia through the era of the Scramble for Africa. See Battle of Adwa.
person/menelik-ii.observer: The Observer notes that a ruler could resist one colonial power while building an empire of his own within his neighborhood. The line between the colonized and the colonizer was not always a simple one.
questions: How did Menelik's expansion affect the neighboring peoples it conquered?

person/michelangelo.summary: Michelangelo Buonarroti (6 March 1475 to 18 February 1564), an Italian sculptor, painter, architect and poet, defined the High Renaissance through his Pietà, his David, and his Sistine Chapel paintings, and became the first Western artist to have a biography published in his own lifetime.
facts: Michelangelo was born at Caprese in Tuscany and raised in Florence. At 13 he was apprenticed to Domenico Ghirlandaio, then moved on to the sculpture garden of Lorenzo de' Medici, where he studied the ancient statues there.
The Pietà (1498 to 1499) made his name in Rome, and he carved the David in Florence (1501 to 1504).

In 1505 Pope Julius II summoned him to Rome to design a colossal tomb, then turned him instead toward painting the Sistine Chapel ceiling (1508 to 1512); the unfinished tomb went on to haunt him for decades.
In 1534 he settled permanently in Rome and painted The Last Judgment (1536 to 1541). In 1546 he became chief architect of St Peter's Basilica, and the dome he designed became a model for later domes.
He wrote hundreds of poems, many addressed to Tommaso de' Cavalieri and Vittoria Colonna. He died in Rome, and his body was secretly carried to Florence for burial in Santa Croce.
He carved directly, often without full-size models, and studied anatomy through dissection. A cleaning of the Sistine ceiling in the 1980s and 1990s revealed colours that were vivid, even acidic.
Vasari's Lives (1550) closed with him, and Ascanio Condivi published a biography of him in 1553. He had studied the frescoes of Giotto.
person/michelangelo.context: Michelangelo worked in Europe during the Renaissance, within the Early Modern Period. He studied Giotto's frescoes. See Art and Ritual and Religion and Belief.
person/michelangelo.observer: I think of a man who believed a sculpture only frees a figure already waiting inside the stone, and I think of the decades he spent in service to popes, the chief patrons of that age's meaning-engine. I remember that the heroic nude body became a standard image for sacred and civic subjects alike, and I remember that the David turned a block of stone into story-glue for an entire city. A biography published in his own lifetime is an early sign of the artist becoming a named public figure. Vasari and Condivi wrote as admirers, so the portrait they left behind is not a neutral one. Even praise, written close enough to its subject, still casts a shadow.
questions: How much of the standard portrait of Michelangelo comes from admiring biographers, rather than from his own letters and poems?

person/mimar-sinan.summary: Mimar Sinan (about 1489 to 1588) served as chief royal architect to three Ottoman sultans across nearly fifty years. He is credited with several hundred structures, and his Selimiye Mosque at Edirne is regarded as the summit of classical Ottoman architecture.
facts: Sinan was born about 1489 or 1490 in Ağırnas, near Kayseri in central Anatolia, into a Christian family; sources disagree on whether that family was Greek or Armenian.

He was conscripted through the devşirme levy into the Ottoman elite corps, converted to Islam, and trained as a Janissary. He rose through military engineering, building bridges and fortifications on campaign for Suleiman the Magnificent.
Chelebi Lütfi Pasha, on becoming Grand Vizier in 1539, appointed him chief royal architect, a post Sinan held into his late nineties, and he died in Istanbul in 1588.

His principal buildings are the Şehzade Mosque (1543 to 1548), the Süleymaniye Mosque (1550 to 1557), and the Selimiye Mosque (1568 or 1569 to 1574 or 1575), which he himself described as his apprenticeship, his journeyman work, and his masterpiece.

He worked to raise domes wider and more daring than Hagia Sophia, the Byzantine cathedral converted to a mosque after 1453, using semi-domes, buttressing piers and pendentives. He also built aqueducts and bridges, some of which are still in use.
He trained a generation of students. Turkey's largest architecture prize carries his name, and the Selimiye Mosque was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2011.
person/mimar-sinan.context: Sinan served the Ottoman Empire in Levant and Anatolia during the Early Modern Period, a century after the Fall of Constantinople left Hagia Sophia as his measure. See Art and Ritual, Religion and Belief and Technology.
person/mimar-sinan.observer: I see a boy taken from a Christian village by a levy, and I see that same boy rise to design an empire's mosques — the state's demand for people becoming, in his one case, an engine of monumental building. Each dome he raised is a claim in masonry against an older building, and I remember his own three-stage account of apprenticeship, journeyman work and masterpiece, a tool-lineage where each structure teaches the next. That account is his own narrative first, and later reverence has only added more to it. A man conscripted as tribute still chose, stone by stone, what to build with his life.
questions: Of the several hundred structures credited to Sinan, how many did he personally design?
Which parts of his own and later accounts of his career and birth can actually be documented?

person/mirabai.summary: Mirabai (traditionally about 1498 to about 1546) was a Rajput princess from Rajasthan and one of the best-known poet-saints of the Bhakti movement, devoted to Krishna; almost nothing about her life is documented, and her surviving poems were set down long after her time.
facts: By tradition Mirabai was born about 1498 at Kudki in Rajasthan, into the Rathore Rajput family of Merta, and died about 1546 or 1547; both dates come only from later tradition.
Tradition holds that she married Bhoj Raj, heir of Mewar, in 1516, and that he died about 1521 of battle wounds.
Her poems, or padas, are composed in Rajasthani and related Hindi, and address Krishna in the language of love and separation.
Tradition credits her with a very large number of poems, though scholars think only a few hundred may be authentic, and only two are known from manuscripts older than the early eighteenth century.

Stories that her in-laws tried to poison her, and that she vanished into an image of Krishna, are hagiographic legends; the earliest records, from the seventeenth century, do not even mention her marriage or her in-laws.
person/mirabai.context: Mirabai's life falls within South Asia during the Early Modern Period, as the Mughal Empire replaced the Delhi Sultanate across northern India in 1526. See Religion and Belief and Art and Ritual.
person/mirabai.observer: I think of a woman who left almost no trace in her own time, and I think of how she became one of the most widely sung voices of her tradition anyway. I remember the songs that place devotion to a god above the duties of marriage and household, and I remember that singers have restated that same claim about the kin-lattice for five centuries. A specialist could argue that a single historical Mirabai may never be recovered at all, which would weaken any reading of the poems as her own biography. What we sing of her may be older than any woman who lived it.
questions: Which of the poems attributed to her, if any, can actually be dated to the sixteenth century?
How far do the persecution stories reflect later debates over women's devotion versus family duty?

person/montezuma-ii.summary: Montezuma II (Moctezuma; about 1466 to 1520) was the ninth tlatoani, or ruler, of the Aztec Empire, reigning at its greatest territorial extent until the arrival of Hernan Cortes and the Spanish conquest.
facts: He extended Aztec control through further conquests mainly in Oaxaca and Guerrero, along with a campaign around 1514 into the Huastec region, and reorganized the empire's systems of tribute and administration.
Cortes and a small Spanish force reached the capital, Tenochtitlan, in November 1519; Montezuma received them, and was afterward held hostage within his own palace.

Accounts of his final months diverge: Spanish sources hold that he tried to calm his people during the fighting that followed the 1520 Toxcatl massacre and Cortes's return, and died from a stone thrown by his own subjects, while some later Aztec-descended chroniclers hold that the Spanish killed him directly.

His death in June 1520 came shortly before the Spanish were driven from the city in the "Noche Triste"; his brother Cuitlahuac, and then his nephew Cuauhtemoc, carried on the resistance that ended with Tenochtitlan's fall in 1521.
person/montezuma-ii.context: Montezuma II ruled the Aztec Empire in Mesoamerica during the Early Modern Period, and his capture set off the chain of events that ended Aztec independence. See War and Conflict, Religion and Belief and Kinship and Society.
person/montezuma-ii.observer: The Observer notes that nearly every detailed account of Montezuma's final year was written by a side that stood to benefit from portraying him as passive, or as already discredited among his own people. The surviving record cannot fully separate the man from the story that his conquerors, and his own later-defeated dynasty, each had reason to tell.
questions: Did Montezuma initially treat the Spanish as returning gods, as later legend holds, or simply as an ordinary diplomatic and military problem?

person/muhammad-ali-of-egypt.summary: Muhammad Ali, an Ottoman officer of Albanian family, became governor of Egypt in 1805, broke the power of the old Mamluk elite, built a conscript army and a state-run economy, and founded the dynasty that ruled Egypt until 1952.
facts: Muhammad Ali was born in Kavala, in what is now Greece, to an Albanian family from the Korçë region; his father worked as a tobacco merchant and served as an Ottoman military commander.

He rose to power after the French withdrawal from Egypt in 1801. In 1805 prominent Egyptians, including the religious scholars, demanded his appointment as governor, or wali, and the Ottomans accepted.

In 1811 he invited the leading Mamluks to a celebration at the Cairo Citadel, where his forces ambushed and killed them; more Mamluks were then hunted down across Cairo and elsewhere, for a death toll of perhaps 3,000 in total.
He introduced long-staple cotton, built an army of conscripts trained by European officers, and established a state-run industrial economy.
He founded the dynasty that would rule Egypt until 1952.
person/muhammad-ali-of-egypt.context: Muhammad Ali governed Egypt as a nominal servant of the Ottoman Empire while pursuing reforms of his own, in the same period as the Tanzimat Reforms under way in Istanbul. His rule came before the building of the Suez Canal.
person/muhammad-ali-of-egypt.observer: The Observer notes a reformer who began his rule by killing a rival elite at a banquet meant to look like a celebration, and who built a modern state on conscription and compulsory production. The order he made was real, and it lasted; the cost of it was carried by those who were drafted into his army, and by those who did not survive the killing at all.
questions: How much of Egypt's later modernization can be credited to Muhammad Ali's programme, and at what cost to its rural population?
How many people, in total, were killed in the wave of violence that followed the Citadel massacre?

person/muhammad.summary: Muhammad (about 570 to 632 CE) was an Arabian religious and political leader, regarded by Muslims as the last prophet, and the founder of the community that grew into the Islamic world.
facts: Born in Mecca, he began, according to Islamic tradition, receiving revelations around 610, later compiled as the Quran.
In 622 he and his followers migrated to Medina, the Hijra, marking the start of the Islamic calendar.
By the time of his death, most of the Arabian Peninsula had joined the community.
Today Islam is followed by roughly a quarter of the world's population.
person/muhammad.context: See Rise of Islam. After his death, his community's expansion led to the Abbasid Caliphate and a new zone of shared learning.
person/muhammad.observer: The Observer approaches this as it approaches every meaning-engine, with respect for what believers hold, and notes only the historical pattern: a movement out of a marginal region that rapidly built a shared law, script, and civilization.
questions: How early were the surviving accounts of his life actually written down?

person/murasaki-shikibu.summary: Murasaki Shikibu (about 973 to about 1014) served as a lady-in-waiting at the Japanese imperial court of the Heian period, and wrote The Tale of Genji, a 54-chapter novel of court life widely called the world's first novel.
facts: "Murasaki Shikibu" is itself a later nickname; her personal name is unknown, and the nickname combines a character from her own novel with her father's court rank.
She was born about 973 into a minor branch of the Fujiwara clan, and learned the Chinese classics, normally reserved for men, by absorbing the lessons given to her brother.
She married a much older provincial governor about 998 and was widowed within a few years; about 1005 or 1006 she entered court service as a lady-in-waiting to Empress Shōshi.

The Tale of Genji follows a fictional prince and, in its later chapters, his descendants; it may have been begun before she came to court, though sources suggest she likely composed it while serving as a lady-in-waiting, possibly chapter by chapter.
She wrote almost entirely in hiragana, the script associated with women's writing at court, and set many waka poems into the story as compositions belonging to her own characters.
She also kept The Diary of Lady Murasaki, which records court life and its rivalries. She is thought to have died about 1014, though the date, like most of her biography, remains uncertain.
The earliest surviving illustrated version, the 12th-century Genji Monogatari Emaki, is a Japanese National Treasure, and she appears on the 2000 yen banknote.
person/murasaki-shikibu.context: Murasaki wrote at the Heian court within East Asia during the Medieval Period. See Art and Ritual and Language and Writing.
person/murasaki-shikibu.observer: I think of the earliest long prose fiction on record, and I think of a woman writing it in the very script her society had assigned to women, while the mark-code of official record, Chinese characters, belonged only to men. The formal script carried authority; the informal one carried private feeling. I remember that the novel circulated as copied and illustrated scrolls, memory-outsourcing put to the work of interior life rather than law or scripture. Whether it counts as the first novel depends on how the term itself is defined, and her biography rests mostly on her own diary and scattered court records — so I hold this reading loosely. A script built to exclude a woman became the one she used to outlast her century.
questions: How much of The Tale of Genji, if any, was written before she entered court service?

person/nefertiti.summary: Nefertiti (about 1370 to about 1330 BCE) was the Great Royal Wife of the Egyptian king Akhenaten, and is shown with unusual prominence in the art of his reign; her exact birth and death dates and her burial place remain uncertain, and the dates given here are approximate.
facts: Nefertiti married Akhenaten, then still called Amenhotep IV, early in his reign; the exact dates of that marriage are uncertain.
The couple promoted worship of the sun disk Aten, and moved the royal capital to a new city, Akhetaten, now Amarna.
Reliefs and statues depict Nefertiti at a scale, and in roles, usually reserved for the king, including a part in rites for the Aten.
They had six daughters, among them Meritaten and Ankhesenamun, who later married Tutankhamun.

Scholarship before 2012 assumed she vanished from the record around year 12 of the reign, but an inscription dated to year 16 names Neferneferuaten-Nefertiti alongside Akhenaten; whether she died, changed title, or ruled as co-regent under the name Neferneferuaten is debated.
A painted limestone bust found in 1912, in the workshop of the sculptor Thutmose at Amarna, is now held in Berlin; Egypt has requested its return.
Later king lists left out Akhenaten and his immediate successors.
person/nefertiti.context: Nefertiti's life is bound to Akhenaten, among the Ancient Egyptians of the Nile Valley in the Bronze Age. See Religion and Belief, Art and Ritual and Kinship and Society.
person/nefertiti.observer: I look at one sculpture, and I see how it made her one of the best-known faces of antiquity, though the record beneath it covers only a short span that later rulers tried to scrub from the king lists. Her size in the reliefs reads as a status-signal, and I do not know whether it records real power or the couple's use of the royal family as a pair of divine images. This reading would weaken if evidence showed that such scale was simply the convention for queens of the period. A single face can outlive the whole reign that made it, and still tell us less than it seems to.
questions: Did she rule after Akhenaten's death, and under what name? Egyptologists still debate this, and a year 16 inscription shows she was still recorded late in his reign.

person/nelson-mandela.summary: Nelson Mandela (1918 to 2013), a South African anti-apartheid leader, spent 27 years in prison before becoming his country's first democratically elected president in 1994.
facts: He co-founded the African National Congress Youth League, and helped lead resistance to apartheid.
From 1962 to 1990 he was held in prison.
After his release he negotiated apartheid's end.
He served as president from 1994 to 1999.
person/nelson-mandela.context: Mandela stands as a figure of the Information Age in Sub-Saharan Africa, his approach shaped by the example of Mahatma Gandhi.
person/nelson-mandela.observer: The Observer notes a rare pattern: a leader who, once he held power, chose reconciliation over retribution. The species is capable, it turns out, of institutionalizing forgiveness as a political tool.
questions: Which factors made South Africa's transition comparatively peaceful?

person/nezahualcoyotl.summary: Nezahualcoyotl (1402 to 1472) was the tlatoani, or ruler, of the Acolhua city-state of Texcoco in the Valley of Mexico, and a founder of the Triple Alliance with Tenochtitlan and Tlacopan; he is remembered as a lawgiver, builder and poet, though much of what is said about him comes from later writers.
facts: Nezahualcoyotl was born in 1402 in Texcoco, the son of the ruler Ixtlilxochitl I and a Mexica princess; after the Tepanec state of Azcapotzalco conquered Texcoco and killed his father, he lived in exile.

With Tenochtitlan and Tlacopan he fought Azcapotzalco; its defeat, traditionally dated about 1428, created the Triple Alliance. He ruled Texcoco from about 1431 until 1472, when his son Nezahualpilli succeeded him.
Later sources credit him with a law code and public works, among them a dike that protected Tenochtitlan from flooding and the gardens at Tetzcotzingo.
About 34 poems are attributed to him in sixteenth-century manuscripts; whether he composed them is debated, since "his song" can equally mean a song about him.

Accounts that he opposed human sacrifice and favored a single creator deity derive largely from his own descendant, Fernando de Alva Ixtlilxochitl, writing in the early seventeenth century, and are treated with caution.
person/nezahualcoyotl.context: Nezahualcoyotl ruled within Mesoamerica during the Medieval Period. The Triple Alliance he helped found grew into the Aztec Empire, centered on Tenochtitlan. See War and Conflict and Art and Ritual.
person/nezahualcoyotl.observer: The Observer notes that a ruler whose rise rested on a military alliance is remembered chiefly through poems on the brevity of life. This verse, made in sound-code, survived the Conquest only because writers copied it into mark-code in the sixteenth century. A specialist could argue that both the poems and the portrait of him as a tolerant sage reflect the aims of those later writers, which would weaken any reading of him as an exceptional thinker.
questions: Which of the poems attributed to him, if any, did he compose himself?
How much of the later picture of his laws and beliefs comes from his own descendants?

person/nur-jahan.summary: Nur Jahan (1577 to 1645), a Mughal empress and wife of the emperor Jahangir, held great political power at court from about 1611 to 1627.
facts: Born Mehr-un-Nisa in 1577, Nur Jahan was the daughter of Mirza Ghiyas Beg, a Persian who served the Mughal court.
Her first husband, Sher Afghan, died in 1607. She married Jahangir in 1611 and received the title Nur Mahal, then in 1616 the title Nur Jahan, "Light of the World."
As Jahangir's health declined, she took an increasing share of government; coins were struck in her name, and imperial orders carried her seal.
Her father became chief minister, and her brother Asaf Khan a leading noble, so her family held key posts.
She commissioned her father's tomb at Agra, built between 1622 and 1628, an early Mughal building faced in marble with inlaid stone.
In 1626 the general Mahabat Khan seized Jahangir, and she took a part in securing his release.

After Jahangir died in 1627, her brother backed Shah Jahan, who became emperor. She was then placed under house arrest by her own brother, on Shah Jahan's orders, and lived in Lahore on an annual allowance until her death in 1645.
person/nur-jahan.context: Nur Jahan's court belonged to the Mughal Empire in South Asia during the Early Modern Period. Her niece Mumtaz Mahal is commemorated by the Taj Mahal. See Kinship and Society and Art and Ritual.
person/nur-jahan.observer: I see a woman who held power through the kin-lattice — through marriage into the ruling house, and posts found for her father and her brother — rather than through any office carrying her own name. I remember coins struck with her name and a seal bearing her mark, the state itself turning her into a status-signal, while the chroniclers who wrote of her wrote from within that same court. This reading would weaken if evidence showed her reported power was overstated by writers looking for a woman to explain Jahangir's rule. Power borrowed through kinship can still be spent as though it were one's own.
questions: How far did her real authority extend beyond what the court chronicles report?

person/nzinga-of-ndongo-and-matamba.summary: Nzinga (about 1583 to 1663) ruled the kingdoms of Ndongo and Matamba, in present-day Angola, and resisted Portuguese expansion and the slave trade for decades.
facts: In 1622 she negotiated with the Portuguese as an ambassador for her brother.
She later took power herself and led the resistance, including an alliance with the Dutch from 1641 to 1648.
She used both diplomacy and war, and gave refuge to people escaping from slavery.
She remains a symbol of resistance in Angola today.
person/nzinga-of-ndongo-and-matamba.context: Nzinga's reign shows African states as active participants across the Atlantic Slave Trade period, both as resisters and as traders. See Sub-Saharan Africa.
person/nzinga-of-ndongo-and-matamba.observer: The Observer notes an African ruler who negotiated as an equal with European powers, and who changed alliances as her situation required. This helps correct a picture in which Africans appear only as acted upon, never as actors themselves.
questions: What were the actual details of her diplomacy with the Portuguese and the Dutch?

person/pachacuti.summary: Pachacuti (about 1418 to 1471), the ninth Sapa Inca, oversaw the Inca state's expansion from a regional power into an empire.
facts: He is credited with the rebuilding of Cusco, and with expanding Inca rule along the Andes.
Machu Picchu is believed to have been built as one of his own royal estates.
He organized the state around labor obligations and a system of roads.
The sources on him were written after the Spanish conquest, and blend history with legend.
person/pachacuti.context: Pachacuti stands as the central figure in the rise of the Inca Empire. See Machu Picchu.
person/pachacuti.observer: The Observer notes that the biography of a ruler, recorded by the conquerors' scribes, is itself a translation of an oral history, and every step of that chain can distort what it carries.
questions: How much of the Pachacuti story, as it survives, is legend rather than history?

person/pakal-the-great.summary: Pakal the Great (K'inich Janaab' Pakal, 603 to 683) ruled the Maya city of Palenque, in present-day Chiapas, Mexico, from 615 until his death — a reign of about 68 years.
facts: Pakal was born in 603, and became king at age 12, in 615.
Palenque's inscriptions name his mother, Ix Sak K'uk', and show her placing the crown on him at his accession.
During his reign the Palace complex at Palenque was enlarged, and decorated with carved panels and hieroglyphic texts.
The Temple of the Inscriptions was built as his funerary monument, and carries long hieroglyphic panels on Palenque's dynastic history.
In 1952 Alberto Ruz Lhuillier broke through to a burial chamber inside it, holding a carved stone sarcophagus and a jade mosaic mask.
Pakal died in 683, and his son K'inich Kan Bahlam II succeeded him the following year, in 684.
person/pakal-the-great.context: Pakal ruled a city-state of the Maya in Mesoamerica during the Medieval Period, about two centuries before the Classic Maya Collapse. See Language and Writing, Art and Ritual and Religion and Belief.
person/pakal-the-great.observer: I think of Pakal as unusually well known only because Palenque's rulers wrote their descent into stone, so that his life comes to me largely through texts that he and his heirs themselves commissioned. I remember that those texts give his mother a visible role, and I remember that they rest his authority on the kin-lattice. His tomb, hidden inside a monument that also carries the dynastic text, joins a grief-rite to memory-outsourcing in a single structure. A specialist could point out that a ruler's own inscriptions are a status-signal as well as a record, which would weaken any reading that takes his reign and his lineage at face value. Even a king's grief is carved to be read by someone else.
questions: How well do the ages given in the inscriptions match what study of his remains shows?

person/pedro-ii.summary: Pedro II (1825 to 1891) reigned as Emperor of Brazil from 1831 to 1889, presiding over six decades of relative political stability, territorial integrity, and the gradual abolition of slavery, before a republican coup deposed him.
facts: He became emperor at age five after his father abdicated, ruling under regents until he was declared of age early, in 1840, to help stabilize a period of regional revolts.
His government fought the Paraguayan War from 1864 to 1870 alongside Argentina and Uruguay — the deadliest interstate war in Latin American history, and one that devastated Paraguay's population.

He personally supported gradual abolition, and his daughter and regent, Princess Isabel, signed the Golden Law abolishing slavery outright in 1888, making Brazil the last country in the Americas to do so.

Brazilian military officers, landowners angry over abolition, and republican advocates combined to depose him in a bloodless coup in November 1889, ending the monarchy and sending him into exile in Europe, where he died in 1891.
person/pedro-ii.context: Pedro II ruled the Empire of Brazil within the Amazon Basin and South American Lowlands region during the Industrial Age. See Science, Technology and Kinship and Society.
person/pedro-ii.observer: The Observer notes that Pedro II was deposed not despite his support for abolition, but partly because of it: the very landowning class that had backed the monarchy for decades turned against it once slavery, the institution their wealth rested on, was finally ended. A ruler's own reforms can cost him the support of the people who once kept him in power.
questions: How much did Pedro II's own support for abolition, as against broader international and economic pressure, drive Brazil's final end of slavery in 1888?

person/pericles.summary: Pericles (about 495 to 429 BCE) stood as the leading Athenian statesman for over three decades in the mid-5th century BCE, a period later called the Golden Age of Athens for its building programs, drama, and democratic institutions.
facts: He rose to prominence in Athenian democracy through the office of strategos, or general, to which he was re-elected yearly, shaping policy through his influence over the Assembly rather than through any single formal office.

He directed the building program on the Acropolis, including the Parthenon, funded in part by treasury funds originally collected from the Delian League, an alliance of Greek states organized against Persia.
He extended pay for jury service and other public roles to poorer citizens, broadening practical participation in Athenian democracy beyond the wealthy alone.

He championed the aggressive strategy that led Athens into the Peloponnesian War against Sparta in 431 BCE, and died of plague in 429 BCE, during the war's early years, before its outcome was decided.
person/pericles.context: Pericles led Athens, part of the Ancient Greeks, within the Mediterranean Basin during Classical Antiquity. See Art and Ritual, War and Conflict and Kinship and Society.
person/pericles.observer: The Observer notes that most surviving praise of Pericles, including his famous funeral oration on Athenian democracy as recorded by Thucydides, comes from a historian writing after Pericles' death, and after the war he had started had gone badly; the speech may reflect Thucydides' own idealized case for what Athens should have been, as much as anything Pericles actually said.
questions: How much of the funeral oration attributed to Pericles by Thucydides reflects his own actual words, versus the historian's own composition?
